args.text: [lane-tern] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System, the internet's address book) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to a server that has moved or been retired, so pages fail or load the wrong content. (2) Slow recovery: when a service switches to a backup server during an outage, cached old answers delay the switch for as long as they last. (3) Lingering bad data: a poisoned or mistaken answer stays in the cache and keeps misdirecting people long after the fix.

[lane-tern] Idempotent (safe to repeat, with the same end result) retries matter because networks drop messages, so a client often cannot tell whether its first request worked. If the retry is idempotent, trying again cannot cause harm such as a double payment or a duplicate order, so systems can recover from failures without human clean-up.

[lane-tern] Two trade-offs of UUIDv7 (Universally Unique Identifier, version 7) as a primary key: (1) Size: it takes 16 bytes, which is larger than a plain whole-number key, so indexes grow and lookups can be slightly slower. (2) Leaked timing: the first part encodes the creation time, so anyone who sees an ID can estimate when the record was made. The upside is that new IDs sort roughly in time order, which keeps database inserts tidier than fully random IDs.

[lane-tern] A write-ahead log (WAL) is a file where a database writes each change before applying it to its main data files. If the system crashes, it replays this log to recover committed changes and undo unfinished ones, so no data is lost or left half-written.

[lane-tern] Two reasons to pin a client version in a benchmark: (1) Fair comparison: a client update can change speed on its own, so results from different runs would reflect the software change rather than the thing being tested. (2) Repeatability: others can rerun the exact setup later and get comparable results, because the client behaves the same way each time.
